title: The Friday Night Protests That Reshaped Civic Participation in Japan
content:
For decades, public protest was something many people in Japan preferred to avoid. However, the anti-nuclear movement that emerged after the Fukushima nuclear disaster changed both who participated in protests and how people were mobilised.

Beginning in March 2012, thousands of people started gathering outside the Prime Minister’s residence in Tokyo to oppose the restart of nuclear power plants. The movement was led by the Metropolitan Coalition Against Nukes (MCAN), a network of 13 small activist groups and independent volunteers campaigning for a phase-out of nuclear power in Japan.

Families with children, students, and many first-time protesters became the face of the movement. At its peak in June 2012, following the government’s decision to restart the Ōi nuclear reactors, participation surged dramatically. On 29 June, an estimated 200,000 people, according to the organisers, gathered around the Prime Minister’s residence, making it one of the largest protest movements Japan had seen in decades. The demonstrations continued almost every Friday for nearly a decade.

title: The Power of the Plenum: Leaderless Student Organising in Serbian and Croatian Student Movements
content:
Explore how leaderless, direct-democratic plenums have worked across student movements from Serbia’s 2026 student blockades to Croatia’s 2009 free-education occupation.

Plenums are open, non-hierarchical discussion and decision-making assemblies where every participant holds an equal voice, enabling movements to make decisions collectively without permanent leaders.

Plenums were used by students in Serbia in 2026, building on precedents such as the 2009 protests in Croatia, when students at the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences in Zagreb staged a monthlong occupation. Below is a collection of guides and articles about this decision making model.

If you have practical guides, reflections, or case studies on plenums to suggest please contact us.

A plenum-type gathering is a first-aid kit for patchwork democracy, rooted in the belief that political change from below is possible. – Suzana Ignjatovic

title: Telling Stories under Oppression: The Power of Textiles in Chile
content:
A powerful illustration of how stories can be told in empowering and engaging ways are arpilleras. Arpilleras are three-dimensional, hand-sewn appliquéd tapestries that “tell a story with each stitch”. They originated in Chile as a medium for women, generally working collectively, to denounce the human rights abuses and repression of the Pinochet dictatorship in Chile.

They have since been used to capture the first-person, lived experience of individuals and communities around the world, in response to war and conflict, and a wide range of other forms of oppression and social injustice.
